title: Work, Energy and Power
lines: Energy methods skip the details of the motion and compare only the start and the end. When a question asks for a speed, height or distance and does not ask for time, try energy first. Take g = 10 m/s².
## Work
- Work done by a constant force: W = Fs cos θ, where θ is the angle between the force and the displacement. Unit: joule (1 J = 1 N·m). Work is a scalar but can be negative.
- θ < 90°: positive work (the force helps the motion). θ = 90°: zero work. θ > 90°: negative work (the force resists).
- The normal force on a body sliding on a fixed surface and the tension in a pendulum string do no work, because they are perpendicular to the motion. A centripetal force never does work.
- Kinetic friction on a body sliding over a fixed surface always does negative work: W = −fs.
- For a varying force, work is the area under the F-x graph. For a spring stretched from 0 to x, W = ½kx².
- The net work is the sum of the works of all forces, or the work of the resultant force.
> Example: A box is dragged 5 m along a floor by a rope pulling with 20 N at 60° above the horizontal. Find the work done by the rope.
! Trap: work by gravity depends only on the change in height, W = mg(h₁ − h₂), not on the path taken.
## Power
- Average power P = W/t; unit watt (1 W = 1 J/s). Instantaneous power P = Fv cos θ, or P = Fv when force and velocity are in line.
- A vehicle with a fixed engine power P has its maximum speed when the driving force equals the resistance: v(max) = P/f.
- At a lower speed v, the driving force is P/v, larger than f, so the vehicle still accelerates: a = (P/v − f)/m.
> Example: A 1000 kg car has engine power 60 kW and faces a constant resistance of 2000 N. Find its top speed and its acceleration at 20 m/s.
! Trap: a car starting at constant power has decreasing acceleration. A car starting at constant acceleration has increasing power until it reaches the rated power; after that its acceleration falls.
## Kinetic energy and the work-energy theorem
- Kinetic energy Eₖ = ½mv², a scalar, never negative. Doubling the speed multiplies Eₖ by 4.
- Work-energy theorem: the total work done by all forces equals the change in kinetic energy, W(net) = ½mv² − ½mu².
- It works for curved paths and varying forces, and is the fastest route for stopping distances.
> Example: A 2 kg block sliding at 6 m/s on a floor with μ = 0.3 comes to rest. How far does it slide?
> Friction = 0.3 × 20 = 6 N. 6 × s = ½ × 2 × 36 = 36, so s = 6 m. Note the mass cancels: s = v²/(2μg) = 36/6 = 6 m.
! Trick: stopping distance under a constant braking force grows with v². Twice the speed means four times the distance.
## Potential energy
- Gravitational potential energy E(p) = mgh, where h is measured from a chosen reference level. The value depends on the reference level; the change does not.
- Gravity's work equals minus the change in potential energy: W(gravity) = −ΔE(p). Going up, gravity does negative work and E(p) increases.
- Elastic potential energy of a spring: E(p) = ½kx², the same for stretch x and compression x.
> Example: A spring with k = 400 N/m is compressed by 0.1 m and launches a 1 kg block across a smooth floor. Find the block's speed.
! Trap: a body below the reference level has negative potential energy. That is allowed; only differences have physical meaning.
## Conservation of mechanical energy
- If only gravity and spring forces do work (no friction, no air resistance, no other driving force), then Eₖ + E(p) is constant: ½mv₁² + mgh₁ = ½mv₂² + mgh₂.
- Normal forces from fixed smooth surfaces and string tensions do no work, so they do not break conservation.
- Speed at the bottom of a smooth slope or curve from height h: v = √(2gh), whatever the shape and whatever the mass.
- For a system (for example two blocks linked over a pulley) use the total energy of the system: the loss of one body's potential energy is shared out as kinetic energy of both.
> Example: A pendulum bob on a 0.8 m string is released from rest with the string horizontal. Find its speed at the lowest point.
> Example: A 3 kg block on a smooth table is joined by a string over the edge pulley to a 1 kg hanging mass. From rest, the hanging mass falls 0.8 m. Find the speed.
> Energy lost by the hanging mass = 1 × 10 × 0.8 = 8 J = ½ × (3 + 1) × v², so v² = 4 and v = 2 m/s.
! Trap: for a single block, mechanical energy is not conserved if the string is doing work on it. Choose the whole system.
## Energy with friction
- With friction, mechanical energy decreases. Work-energy: initial mechanical energy − energy lost to friction = final mechanical energy.
- The heat produced by sliding friction is Q = f × (relative sliding distance between the two surfaces), not the distance either body moves relative to the ground.
> Example: A 2 kg block slides from rest down a rough curved ramp of height 5 m and reaches the bottom at 8 m/s. Find the work done against friction.
> mgh = 100 J, Eₖ at the bottom = ½ × 2 × 64 = 64 J, so 36 J was turned into heat.
> Example: A 1 kg block is placed on a long board. Sliding friction between them is 4 N and the block slides 1.5 m relative to the board before they move together. Find the heat produced.
> Q = f × relative distance = 4 × 1.5 = 6 J, whatever distances the block and board each move over the ground.
## Efficiency
- Efficiency η = useful output energy ÷ total input energy = useful power ÷ input power, always less than 100 % in real machines.
> Example: A motor with an input power of 500 W lifts a 50 kg load by 6 m at constant speed in 10 s. Find its efficiency.
! Trap: lifting "at constant speed" means the lifting force equals mg, so useful work is just mgh, with no kinetic energy term.
## Exam checklist
- No time asked? Use energy. A collision in the middle? Use momentum there, energy elsewhere.
- List which forces do work; decide whether mechanical energy is conserved.
- Keep signs: friction and resistance do negative work.
